svg.title: Bench bring-up — what to buy, what the VUSB cut does, and the order to prove things in
svg.desc: Companion to the breadboard wiring figure. Panels covering the board and sensor counts, what the VUSB to VIN cut does to USB power, the five-step bring-up order, and the checks to make before any wire goes in.
svg.text: Bench bring-up — read this before and after, not while wiring
Companion to breadboard-layout. That figure is the wiring; this one is the counts, the rules and the order.
Three boards per station — and nothing more to order
9 breadboards = 3 stations × 3 boards. Exactly what was ordered.
AS5600 ×5 covers it, because the bench unit is the one you then fit
to that vehicle — better anyway, since AGC is tuned per part.

text.tspan: The drive board needs no AS5600; the steering board needs no latches.

svg.text: Splitting them costs one breadboard and buys a harness-shaped bench.
Jumper sets ×3 — one per station — is also right.
Nothing on these boards may carry coil current. No relay, no MOSFET,
no 12 V. Signal on breadboard, authority on soldered perfboard.
After the VUSB–VIN cut: USB is data only
Yes. The laptop still programs the board and still carries
micro-ROS. It just cannot power it. 5 V comes from a UBEC
into VIN, on the bench and on the vehicle alike.
The cut exists so the laptop's 5 V and the UBEC's 5 V
never meet and push current into each other through
the Teensy.

text.tspan: A Teensy that seems dead on USB after the cut is

svg.text: working correctly. Tape a note inside the parts box.
Prove it in this order — each step fails for a different reason
1 · Power only. 5 V at VIN. Meter the + rail on board C, the far end of the chain: 3.3 V there proves the 3V3 pin, both rail
bridges and both board-to-board feeds in one reading. Not there → a wire, not a sensor.
2 · Latches, on a meter, before any code. Probe each OUT against GND and pass a magnet by. It must snap between 0 V
and 3.3 V and stay there when the magnet leaves — that is what makes it a latch. Falls back on its own → it is a switch, and
the whole quadrature scheme is wrong. Flip the magnet to reset it.
3 · I²C scan. 0x36 must appear, and nothing else — one device per bus is the design.
4 · AGC. Read 0x1A at the working gap, tune to mid-scale, and write the gap down — it is the number the other two
vehicles are built to.
5 · Counts last. Bring up the decoder and move a magnet past both latches in sequence. Up one way and down the other
is the first proof the (n + ½) spacing is right — cheap here, expensive on a wheel.

text.tspan: Steps 1–3 need no firmware beyond a scan sketch. If something is wrong, it is wrong before code can be blamed.

svg.text: Before a single wire goes in
The TO-92 pin order is not guessable. Reversed VCC/GND destroys the part — that is what the fourteen spares are for, and it is
a far cheaper lesson on a breadboard than on a soldered board. Bend the legs out to 2.54 mm before inserting.
Keep them in the labelled bag until each one is fitted. TI marks a TO-92 body with an abbreviated code, so loose parts are
unidentifiable and BC looks exactly like AG.
Beep the three boards' − rails together before powering up. A missing ground reads as a dead sensor, and on the vehicle
this same joint becomes the star ground at the motor driver.
